name: atomic_queue
workload: SPSC round-trip ping-pong: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte int counter 1,000,000 times via two queue instances (lowest-contention case); also an N-producer/N-consumer throughput scalability test moving 1,000,000 messages through one queue, run across AMD Ryzen 5950X, Ryzen 5825U, Intel i9-9900KS and Intel Xeon Gold 6132.
claimed_speedup: AtomicQueue mean round-trip latency 42ns vs std::mutex 320ns on Ryzen 5950X (~7.6x lower); OptimistAtomicQueue 33ns (~9.7x lower). At 1-producer/1-consumer throughput: AtomicQueue 142.7M msg/s vs std::mutex 4.1M msg/s (~34x); OptimistAtomicQueue reports up to ~1.23B msg/s in the same 1P/1C cell, which is an implausible outlier (see caveats).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0 (primary systems; gcc-8.4.0 on legacy i9-9900KS/Xeon Gold systems); Makefile release flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -std=c++14 -falign-functions=64 -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Ryzen 5825U (KDE Neon/Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, mitigations=off); legacy: Intel i9-9900KS (Kubuntu 18.04) and Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (RHEL 6.10)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile/construction time (ring buffer, no heap growth); no OS-blocking wait, only busy-spin (push/pop can't sleep, unsuitable for non-latency-critical code that wants to yield the CPU); atomic-element variants reserve a NIL sentinel value that must never be pushed; value-semantics only (copies/moves elements, no in-place references).
caveats: The 1P/1C throughput cell for OptimistAtomicQueue (~1.23B msg/s, stdev ~135M) is far above what its own 42/33ns latency numbers would imply and is almost certainly a measurement/compiler-hoisting artifact of the fully uncontended, dependency-free loop rather than a sustained rate; treat the 7.6-9.7x latency figures as the solid claim and discount the >200x throughput figure. Throughput scaling is also non-monotonic across some thread counts (e.g. std::mutex briefly outperforms AtomicQueue at exactly 2 threads on the 5950X), which the author's own charts show and do not hide.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "atomic queue" --sort stars (seed-query variation of 'lock-free queue benchmark vs std::mutex std::queue'); opened repo README which links to the benchmarks.html shootout page

name: moodycamel::ReaderWriterQueue
workload: Same third-party SPSC round-trip ping-pong benchmark as the atomic_queue shootout: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte counter via two queue instances, 1,000,000 round trips, on AMD Ryzen 5950X.
claimed_speedup: moodycamel::ReaderWriterQueue mean round-trip latency 43ns vs std::mutex mean 320ns -> ~7.4x lower latency. (Evidence is from an independent third-party shootout, not the project's own benchmark -- the project's own blog post benchmarks only compare it against another SPSC queue and folly::ProducerConsumerQueue, not std::mutex.)
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0; -O3 -march=native -mtune=native (atomic_queue project's release Makefile flags, used uniformly for all compared queues including readerwriterqueue commit 2ae710d)
tradeoffs: Strictly single-producer/single-consumer only (roles can't switch); non-blocking try_enqueue never allocates but plain enqueue can grow the queue dynamically; blocking variant (BlockingReaderWriterQueue) adds wait_dequeue but destroying the queue while a thread waits on it is undefined behaviour.
caveats: Its own project blog post (moodycamel.com, 2013-2015 benchmarks, GCC 4.7-4.9/MSVC2010/ICC13 on a Linode Xeon L5520 VM) never benchmarks against std::mutex+std::queue at all, only against another SPSC queue and folly; the std::mutex comparison used here comes entirely from the independent max0x7ba/atomic_queue shootout.
found_via: GitHub: found as one of the reference baselines in max0x7ba/atomic_queue's benchmarks.html shootout (reached via seed-query variation 'atomic queue' / 'lock-free queue')

name: Boost.Lockfree
workload: Same third-party SPSC/MPMC round-trip ping-pong benchmark as the atomic_queue shootout, on AMD Ryzen 5950X; boost::lockfree::spsc_queue used in the SPSC role, boost::lockfree::queue in the MPMC role.
claimed_speedup: boost::lockfree::spsc_queue mean round-trip latency 51ns vs std::mutex 320ns -> ~6.3x lower; boost::lockfree::queue (MPMC-capable) 92ns -> ~3.5x lower. A separate, older, independent benchmark from Qihoo 360's evpp project (2015, GCC 4.8.2, Xeon E5-2630 v2) found boost::lockfree::queue throughput 100%-500% higher than std::mutex+std::vector under multiple producers, corroborating the win on different hardware/vintage.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0; -O3 -march=native -mtune=native (atomic_queue shootout); corroborating evpp benchmark used gcc-4.8.2
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X, Linux, mitigations=off (primary); Intel Xeon E5-2630 v2 / CentOS 6.2 (corroborating evpp benchmark)
stars_or_usage: 160 stars on the standalone mirror repo; ships as part of Boost, one of the most widely deployed C++ library collections
tradeoffs: boost::lockfree::queue requires either a bounded capacity or a lock-free allocator for unbounded use; elements generally need to be trivially copyable / POD-like for best behaviour; API and iterator semantics differ substantially from std::queue.
caveats: Evidence is a third-party shootout plus a second, much older (2015) independent benchmark from a production codebase (evpp) -- neither is Boost.Lockfree's own published benchmark. The evpp benchmark's largest 'winner' was actually moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue (already catalogued, excluded here); Boost.Lockfree was the second-best performer there.
found_via: GitHub: found as one of the reference baselines in max0x7ba/atomic_queue's benchmarks.html shootout; corroborated via web search hit on Qihoo360/evpp/docs/benchmark_lockfree_vs_mutex.md

name: xenium
workload: Same third-party SPSC/MPMC round-trip ping-pong benchmark as the atomic_queue shootout, on AMD Ryzen 5950X; xenium's michael_scott_queue, ramalhete_queue and vyukov_bounded_queue implementations were each run in place of the SPSC/MPMC queue.
claimed_speedup: xenium::ramalhete_queue mean round-trip latency 56ns vs std::mutex 320ns -> ~5.7x lower; xenium::vyukov_bounded_queue 60ns (~5.3x lower); xenium::michael_scott_queue 128ns (~2.5x lower).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0; -O3 -march=native -mtune=native (atomic_queue shootout's release Makefile flags, applied uniformly to xenium commit f6416d3)
tradeoffs: Requires choosing a memory-reclamation scheme (hazard pointers, epoch-based, etc.) as a template parameter, which adds API and mental overhead versus std::mutex+std::queue; michael_scott_queue and ramalhete_queue are unbounded (allocate nodes), vyukov_bounded_queue is fixed-capacity; header-only but template-heavy, can affect compile times.
caveats: Evidence is entirely from the independent max0x7ba/atomic_queue shootout, not from xenium's own repo (which has no README benchmark section vs std::mutex). Repo has had no commits in over a year (last push 2025-07-29), so treat as stale rather than actively maintained, though the code itself is described by other users as feature-complete.
found_via: GitHub: found as one of the reference baselines in max0x7ba/atomic_queue's benchmarks.html shootout

name: oneTBB concurrent_bounded_queue
workload: Same third-party SPSC/MPMC round-trip ping-pong benchmark as the atomic_queue shootout, on AMD Ryzen 5950X; tbb::concurrent_bounded_queue used in non-blocking mode.
claimed_speedup: tbb::concurrent_bounded_queue mean round-trip latency 83ns vs std::mutex mean 320ns -> ~3.9x lower latency.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0; -O3 -march=native -mtune=native (atomic_queue shootout's release Makefile flags, applied to TBB 2021.11.0-2ubuntu2)
stars_or_usage: 6.7k stars; Intel's production threading library, widely used in industry (e.g. in numerous HPC and media codebases)
tradeoffs: Pulls in the whole oneTBB dependency/runtime (task scheduler, allocators) rather than being a header-only drop-in; concurrent_bounded_queue's blocking pop() differs in semantics from std::queue and needs care around abort()/cancellation; heavier binary/link footprint than a single-header queue.
caveats: Evidence is from the independent max0x7ba/atomic_queue shootout rather than oneTBB's own published benchmarks; oneTBB is a large general-purpose parallelism library, so this result speaks only to its bounded-queue component, not the library as a whole.
found_via: GitHub: found as one of the reference baselines in max0x7ba/atomic_queue's benchmarks.html shootout
